results.corrected_extracted: The authors call identifying others' emotions an important first step in empathy, and describe their earlier imaging study (Bedi et al., 2009) as finding no change in the accuracy of identifying emotions in faces, whose expressions were not subtle and were shown for 4 seconds. They suggest the new pattern may be more consistent with increased social approach than with increased empathy: MDMA may ease social interaction by reducing the impact of others' negative emotions rather than by improving recognition of them. Limits they name: static photographs may be less true to life than moving faces; no task compared social with non-social pictures; the methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight; all participants had used ecstasy before, so the findings may not apply to people new to MDMA.
results.note: All content confirmed. The cited Discussion paragraph (p. 6) hedges: the pattern 'may be more consistent' with social approach; the hedge is restored (only the abstract states it unhedged).

results.corrected_extracted: 10 men and 10 women had sometimes taken cannabis with MDMA and said the main effect of adding it was more desire; the ratings were said to refer to MDMA alone, and the authors report no difference in any rating between those who did and did not add cannabis, without data. The Discussion calls the effects on erection inconsistent, while the Summary reports erection impaired in 40% of the men without the 40% who reported better erections, and the conclusion says MDMA seems to impair sexual performance in spite of more desire and the perception of greater satisfaction. Limits named by the authors: a sample not randomly selected, of people willing to describe use of an illegal drug; retrospective recall open to inaccuracy; unknown dose and purity of the pills; cannabis use by about half; and expected effects of the drug (a placebo effect), which should not be disregarded.
results.note: Results p. 128: users said cannabis's main effect was more desire, an effect report, not a stated aim (the aim is the authors' reading, Discussion). Restored 'the perception of' greater satisfaction (pp. 127, 129). Rest confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Qualitative study reported by a single author: face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews of 1 to 2 hours, taped and transcribed, conducted by four trained interviewers (two of them the project directors) with current and former ecstasy users in Northern Ireland, October 1997 to November 1998; 106 interviewed and 8 discarded for recording or transcription problems, leaving 98. Recruited through notices in shops and health centres, a club and music magazine, local agencies (including sexually transmitted disease clinics and gay and lesbian outreach), the interviewers' own contacts, referral by respondents and paid recruiters (10 pounds per referral and completed interview); clubs were not used. 69% men; aged 17 to 45 (mean 25); 16% gay or bisexual; 92% had used ecstasy in the past 6 months and 44% on at least 100 occasions. Effects attributed to MDMA refer to what respondents believed they had taken, as tablet content varies. The article describes no method of analysis and counts no finding.

results.corrected_extracted: Several respondents who had sex during ecstasy episodes, more often those aged about 18 to 25, described behaviours carrying a risk of infection: multiple partners and one-night stands with strangers or distant acquaintances; a number voiced regret the next day. Condom use was rare during ecstasy episodes that involved intercourse, but few respondents reported using condoms when no drugs had been taken either. Asked whether ecstasy or alcohol brought more sexual risk, respondents gave mixed views; because a number of respondents took alcohol and other substances in the same episodes, the author says their effects are hard to disentangle.
results.note: Content confirmed (p. 1471-1472). Next-day regret was listed as an infection-risk behaviour; separated. Condom use without drugs kept as respondents' report.

results.corrected_extracted: Interactions of MDMA with alcohol and cannabis could not be examined, and the author says prospective data might be needed, with detailed timing of drug use and sex, as recall of heavy multi-drug episodes may be affected. The abstract states findings more strongly than the text: most respondents (the text: a slight majority) reported closeness without wanting penetrative sex; gay and bisexual women in particular had used MDMA for sexual enhancement, which the Discussion says their small number in the sample does not allow to be concluded; and sexual risk taking was prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, without counts and without the finding that condoms were also rare without drugs. The data are from 1997 and 1998; the author says the scene has probably changed and that it is unclear whether the findings apply now.
results.note: All confirmed except the hedge: the source says prospective data 'might be needed' (p. 1473), not 'would be needed'.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors call the dose relatively small (stating, without a source, that street ecstasy frequently contains more than 100 mg), say the rise came at a time of day when vasopressin would not be expected to change, and conclude that the low-sodium illness is likely linked to MDMA's ability to stimulate vasopressin secretion, that with excessive fluid even a small dose could lead to symptoms, and that the rise does not seem to be part of a general stress response because cortisol did not change significantly. The letter tested neither of the first two conclusions: it gave no fluid load, measured no urine and studied no illness; the third rests on a non-significant cortisol rise in 8 men; and its closing message about fluid intake and its statement on thirst and judgement rest on no data from the study.

MDMA against alcohol: asked which brought more sexual risk, respondents were mixed; some said risk was greater on ecstasy, others that alcohol was far more likely to lead to risk and that they felt more in control on ecstasy; because a number of respondents took alcohol and other substances in the same episodes, the author says their effects are difficult to disentangle. (Source: 'difficult to disentangle', p. 1472, not 'could not be'.)

Limitations stated: the data are from 1997 and 1998 and the scene has probably changed (tablet prices, by anecdotal report, fell from about 10 to 5 pounds; researchers in England report more alcohol use in clubs, and the author says similar changes are possible in Northern Ireland), so it is unclear whether the findings apply now; prospective data, with the timing of substance use and sex, might be needed. (pp. 1473-1474: the alcohol change is England's and only 'possible' locally; 'might be needed'.)

Context from footnotes: clubs were not used for recruitment because local folklore tied some paramilitary groups to clubs and recruiting there might have raised suspicion and put respondents and researchers at risk; respondents said some clubs turned off water taps in toilets, and in several clubs only bottled water was sold; respondents said they recognised people on MDMA by large black pupils, clenched teeth, an 'irregular' jaw formation and extreme friendliness, particularly with strangers. (Footnote e says 'local folklore suggests', not 'reported links'.)

(Source: 'probably because of'.) Note checked: 8 pairs give p = 0.63; p = 0.1 fits about 64 pooled samples two-tailed, or about 42 if one-tailed like the letter's other tests.

My reading at 600 dpi agrees: AVP after MDMA about 1.5, 3.1, 4.1, 2.8 and 1.5 pmol/L at 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 h; controls about 1.3 before and 0.6-0.95 from 1 to 8 h; both about 1.76 at 24 h; MDMA about 45 and 47 micrograms per litre at 2 and 4 h; asterisks beside the 1, 2 and 4 h AVP points. The legend's 'geometric means' may apply to MDMA as well.

Authors' conclusions: the rise in AVP with a small fall in sodium makes hyponatraemic illness after ecstasy likely to be linked to the drug's ability to stimulate AVP secretion; with excessive fluid intake even a relatively small dose could lead to symptoms; the rise does not seem to be part of a generalised stress response because cortisol did not change significantly; animal studies show that MDMA releases serotonin and that serotonergic pathways regulate AVP secretion. (Source: 'does not seem to be part of'.)

reporting_issues.correction: Recomputed: r = 0.2 with 8 pairs gives p = 0.63; p = 0.1 needs about 64 samples two-tailed or about 42 one-tailed.

But 'claimed' drops two of the authors' hedges: the rise 'does not seem to be' part of a stress response, and 'It therefore seems' that hyponatraemia results from a pharmacological effect plus fluid (4th paragraph); restore them.

missed: The authors' answer to time-of-day confounding is an uncited statement that AVP would not be expected to change at that time of day (4th paragraph); their own 3 control occasions show AVP falling to about 0.6 pmol/L and then rising to about 1.76 by 24 h, so it does vary over the day.

hysek_check.note: p. 1647, right column: the inequality-aversion test is reported 'in subjects with a prosocial orientation' (F(1,20) = 3.39, P = 0.079); only their number is missing. The card's 'which volunteers' wording should become 'how many'.

Holds: my reading of Figure 4E from the PDF's vector coordinates gives mean-curve peaks of 182.7 ng/mL (men) and 193.8 (women), both at 2.5 h (identical to the point's 183 and 194); the sex difference in the figure is far smaller; the paper does not explain it; F(1,15) is printed for 16 against 16. Adjust the reasoning: a mean of individual Cmax values always exceeds the peak of the averaged curve, because people peak at different times, so the Cmax gap alone is not an inconsistency. AUC is the clean test, since the area under the mean curve equals the mean of the individual areas: editors' trapezoid AUC0-6h from the plotted means is about 866 (men) and 921 (women) ng/mL h against the printed 926.8 and 1146.5. So the text and figure do disagree, mainly for women (about 20%).

My readings from vector coordinates (placebo then MDMA): explicit all 4.40/5.01, women 4.96/5.15, men 3.84/4.87 (point: 3.9 and 5.2, within rounding); implicit all 4.30/4.81, women 4.79/4.79, men 3.81/4.83; cognitive 62.3/61.9%; SVO all 31.2/36.9, women 36.8/36.6, men 25.7/37.2 degrees; inequality-aversion index all 0.48/0.38 (women 0.44/0.34, men 0.54/0.42); oxytocin change 12.2/65.9 pg/mL.
